title: Firewall Rule Hit Tracking (iptables/nftables)
exclusions: Measures cumulative packet and byte counters for explicitly managed Linux nftables or iptables rules. It does not parse UFW/Netfilter log messages, identify source or destination endpoints, prove that a packet was accepted or dropped, count unique connections, reconstruct payload bytes, detect firewall-policy changes, or establish malicious intent or regulatory compliance. One packet can increment several rule counters as it traverses chains, so totals must not be added across rules and called unique traffic. The reference collector covers nftables inline anonymous counters and iptables/ip6tables rule counters carrying a unique `splunk-rule-id`; nftables named counters, sets/maps with shared counters, eBPF firewalls, firewalld abstractions, hardware offload counters, and unmanaged rules are outside scope. An identical iptables rule deleted and recreated between polls cannot be distinguished if its position, fingerprint, and resulting counter are all indistinguishable at both snapshots.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_firewall_rule_counter_delta_5m` saved-report definition, dispatch history, collector and search-app versions, identity registry, and exported result rows containing `host`, `boot_id`, `backend`, `family`, `table`, `chain`, `rule_id`, `rule_fingerprint`, `native_rule_key`, `window_start`, `window_end`, `packets_delta`, `bytes_delta`, `packets_per_second`, `bytes_per_second`, `observed_intervals`, `measured_intervals`, and `reset_intervals`. These artifacts demonstrate counter collection and calculation; they do not prove packet disposition, threat activity, production validation, or compliance.

controlTest.positiveScenario: For `host=fw-positive`, index six one-minute `linux:firewall_rule_counter` JSON events under one `boot_id` and the same complete rule identity. Use `backend=nftables`, `family=inet`, `table=filter`, `chain=input`, `rule_id=allow-ssh`, `rule_fingerprint=test-fingerprint`, and `native_rule_key=handle:17`. Starting at 1,000 packets and 100,000 bytes, increase each adjacent sample by exactly 10 packets and 1,000 bytes. Five candidate intervals must yield `packets_delta=50`, `bytes_delta=5000`, `measured_intervals=5`, `reset_intervals=0`, `elapsed_seconds=300`, and `measurement_state=hits`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Repeat the six-event sequence for `host=fw-zero` without increasing either cumulative counter; the report must classify the row as `no_hits` with zero packet and byte deltas, not as missing data. In a separate sequence, decrease either cumulative counter on the third candidate interval; that interval must increment `reset_intervals`, must not contribute a packet or byte delta, and must make `measurement_state=counter_reset` rather than interpreting a negative value, wrap, or post-reset value as traffic.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=linux:firewall_rule_counter source=linux_firewall_rule_counter` newline-delimited JSON from a deployment-owned Universal Forwarder scripted input at 60-second cadence. For native nftables, the collector reads `nft --json list ruleset` and selects rules with one inline counter and a `splunk-rule-id=<id>` rule comment. For the iptables interface, it reads exact cumulative packet/byte values from `iptables-save --counters` and `ip6tables-save --counters` and selects rules with an xtables comment containing the same ID. Every event includes sample time, boot ID, backend, family, table, chain, logical rule ID, rule fingerprint, native rule locator, packets, and bytes.
app: A deployment-owned scripted-input app (example name `TA_linux_firewall_counters`) on Linux Universal Forwarders. No Splunkbase app supplies the normalized counter feed or rule-identity contract used by this UC.

| where isnotnull(sample_epoch) AND sample_epoch>0 AND isnotnull(packets_total) AND packets_total>=0 AND isnotnull(bytes_total) AND bytes_total>=0 AND isnotnull(boot_id) AND isnotnull(backend) AND isnotnull(family) AND isnotnull(table) AND isnotnull(chain) AND isnotnull(rule_id) AND isnotnull(rule_fingerprint) AND isnotnull(native_rule_key)

| streamstats current=f window=1 last(sample_epoch) as previous_sample_epoch last(packets_total) as previous_packets_total last(bytes_total) as previous_bytes_total by host boot_id backend family table chain rule_id rule_fingerprint native_rule_key
| eval elapsed_seconds=sample_epoch-previous_sample_epoch

| eval packets_delta=if(comparable_interval=1 AND counter_reset=0,packets_total-previous_packets_total,null()), bytes_delta=if(comparable_interval=1 AND counter_reset=0,bytes_total-previous_bytes_total,null())
| where comparable_interval=1
| eval candidate_start=relative_time(now(),"-9m@m"), candidate_end=relative_time(now(),"-4m@m")
| where sample_epoch>=candidate_start AND sample_epoch<candidate_end
| stats sum(packets_delta) as packets_delta sum(bytes_delta) as bytes_delta count as observed_intervals count(packets_delta) as measured_intervals sum(counter_reset) as reset_intervals sum(elapsed_seconds) as elapsed_seconds min(previous_sample_epoch) as window_start max(sample_epoch) as window_end latest(rule_comment) as rule_comment by host boot_id backend family table chain rule_id rule_fingerprint native_rule_key
| eval packets_delta=coalesce(packets_delta,0), bytes_delta=coalesce(bytes_delta,0), measured_seconds=if(reset_intervals=0,elapsed_seconds,null())
| eval packets_per_second=if(measured_seconds>0,packets_delta/measured_seconds,null()), bytes_per_second=if(measured_seconds>0,bytes_delta/measured_seconds,null())

| eval packets_per_second=round(packets_per_second,3), bytes_per_second=round(bytes_per_second,3)
| convert ctime(window_start) ctime(window_end)
| sort 0 host backend family table chain rule_id
description: Produces a five-minute, per-rule ledger of packet and byte increases from adjacent cumulative nftables or iptables snapshots. The search preserves host, boot, backend, namespace, operator-assigned rule ID, semantic fingerprint, and native locator as the rule-instance key; rejects nonnumeric values and long collection gaps; and reports counter decreases as resets instead of traffic. Zero deltas remain visible as `no_hits` because an unused rule is a valid measurement, not an absent event.
value: Reliable rule-level hit deltas show which controls are exercised, which rules may be stale, and where policy ordering or unexpected traffic deserves investigation without enabling a log action on every packet. Explicit identity and unit handling make the results suitable for firewall tuning and operational review while avoiding the false precision of treating syslog line counts, cumulative totals, or summed chain counters as unique network activity.
implementation: Assign stable, unique `splunk-rule-id` comments to the rules in scope, enable an inline `counter` on each selected nftables rule, or retain the native iptables counters. Deploy the reference collector in a dedicated Universal Forwarder app, select exactly one backend interface per host, run it every 60 seconds with read-only ruleset access, and extract its JSON at search time. Save the supplied SPL as a five-minute report. Treat packet and byte thresholds as local policy layered on the measured deltas, not Netfilter or Splunk defaults.
scriptExample:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import copy
import hashlib
import json
import re
import shlex
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from collections import defaultdict

ID_RE = re.compile(r"(?:^|[ ])splunk-rule-id=([A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:-]{0,127})(?:[ ]|$)")
COUNTER_RE = re.compile("^" + re.escape("[") + "([0-9]+):([0-9]+)" + re.escape("]") + "$")
BOOT_ID_FILE = "/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id"


def command(argv):
    return subprocess.run(argv, check=True, text=True, capture_output=True).stdout


def rule_id(comment):
    match = ID_RE.search(comment or "")
    return match.group(1) if match else None


def fingerprint(value):
    encoded = json.dumps(value, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(encoded).hexdigest()


def emit(sample_epoch, boot_id, backend, family, table, chain, logical_id,
         rule_fingerprint, native_rule_key, packets, byte_count, comment):
    event = {
        "sample_epoch": sample_epoch,
        "boot_id": boot_id,
        "backend": backend,
        "family": family,
        "table": table,
        "chain": chain,
        "rule_id": logical_id,
        "rule_fingerprint": rule_fingerprint,
        "native_rule_key": native_rule_key,
        "packets_total": packets,
        "bytes_total": byte_count,
        "rule_comment": comment,
        "collector_version": 1,
    }
    print(json.dumps(event, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")))


def collect_nft(sample_epoch, boot_id):
    document = json.loads(command(["nft", "--json", "list", "ruleset"]))
    for item in document.get("nftables", []):
        rule = item.get("rule") if isinstance(item, dict) else None
        if not isinstance(rule, dict):
            continue
        comment = str(rule.get("comment", ""))
        logical_id = rule_id(comment)
        counters = []
        for expression in rule.get("expr", []):
            if isinstance(expression, dict) and isinstance(expression.get("counter"), dict):
                counter = expression["counter"]
                if "packets" in counter and "bytes" in counter:
                    counters.append(counter)
        if logical_id is None or len(counters) != 1 or "handle" not in rule:
            continue
        canonical = copy.deepcopy(rule)
        canonical.pop("handle", None)
        canonical.pop("index", None)
        for expression in canonical.get("expr", []):
            counter = expression.get("counter") if isinstance(expression, dict) else None
            if isinstance(counter, dict):
                counter.pop("packets", None)
                counter.pop("bytes", None)
        counter = counters[0]
        emit(sample_epoch, boot_id, "nftables", str(rule["family"]),
             str(rule["table"]), str(rule["chain"]), logical_id,
             fingerprint(canonical), "handle:" + str(rule["handle"]),
             int(counter["packets"]), int(counter["bytes"]), comment)


def comment_from_tokens(tokens):
    for index, token in enumerate(tokens[:-1]):
        if token == "--comment":
            return tokens[index + 1]
    return ""


def collect_iptables(sample_epoch, boot_id):
    for family, executable in (("ip", "iptables-save"), ("ip6", "ip6tables-save")):
        table = None
        positions = defaultdict(int)
        for raw_line in command([executable, "--counters"]).splitlines():
            if raw_line.startswith("*"):
                table = raw_line[1:]
                continue
            if table is None or not raw_line.startswith("["):
                continue
            tokens = shlex.split(raw_line)
            if len(tokens) < 3 or COUNTER_RE.fullmatch(tokens[0]) is None or tokens[1] != "-A":
                continue
            counter_match = COUNTER_RE.fullmatch(tokens[0])
            chain = tokens[2]
            positions[(table, chain)] += 1
            comment = comment_from_tokens(tokens)
            logical_id = rule_id(comment)
            if logical_id is None:
                continue
            rule_tokens = tokens[1:]
            emit(sample_epoch, boot_id, "iptables", family, table, chain,
                 logical_id, fingerprint(rule_tokens),
                 "position:" + str(positions[(table, chain)]),
                 int(counter_match.group(1)), int(counter_match.group(2)), comment)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2 or sys.argv[1] not in {"nftables", "iptables"}:
        raise SystemExit("usage: linux_firewall_rule_counter.py nftables|iptables")
    with open(BOOT_ID_FILE, encoding="ascii") as handle:
        boot_id = handle.read().strip()
    sample_epoch = int(time.time())
    if sys.argv[1] == "nftables":
        collect_nft(sample_epoch, boot_id)
    else:
        collect_iptables(sample_epoch, boot_id)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

knownFalsePositives:
This UC is a measurement report, so a hit is not inherently an alert or a false positive. If consumers add a high-hit or newly-active policy, review these legitimate causes before escalation:

1. **Approved vulnerability scans and monitoring probes** — Repeated connection attempts can legitimately exercise reject, rate-limit, or allow rules. Correlate the exact rule and window with the scanner inventory and change ticket; do not suppress all traffic from a broad source range.

2. **Health checks, service discovery, and retry storms** — Load balancers, orchestrators, and clients with aggressive retries can create real packet hits without hostile intent. Compare destination service health and deployment events before changing firewall policy.

3. **Backup, replication, patching, or failover windows** — Scheduled workflows can activate rules that are quiet during ordinary operation. Maintain host-class and rule-specific baselines rather than a catalogue-wide packet threshold.

4. **Rule-order and chain-traversal effects** — A packet can increment counters in several chains or earlier nonterminating rules. Each counter is correct for that rule, but summing them overstates unique packets. Investigate traversal semantics instead of deduplicating by arithmetic.

5. **Duplicate or mixed collectors** — Polling both nftables and the iptables-nft compatibility interface can describe the same kernel rules twice. Select one declared backend per host. Duplicate forwarders with the same `host` can also create contradictory snapshots; verify forwarder identity and deployment ownership.

6. **Counter reset or ruleset reload** — Maintenance can reset counters or replace native rule instances. The SPL labels a decrease as `counter_reset` and excludes that interval from rates. A reset is data quality/change context, not zero traffic and not a burst.

7. **Rule identity reuse** — Reusing one `splunk-rule-id` for two rules or changing rule semantics without governance splits or confuses history. Require uniqueness per host/backend namespace and review fingerprint changes as configuration events.

**Suppression mechanism:** the primary SPL has no exception lookup and should retain zero-hit and reset rows. If a downstream alert requires suppression, apply it only after delta calculation and key it by exact `host`, `backend`, `family`, `table`, `chain`, `rule_id`, bounded start/end epochs, owner, reason, ticket, and expiry. Preserve the unsuppressed measurement; never filter raw snapshots before `streamstats`, because doing so can splice nonadjacent cumulative counters.
mitreAttack: N/A (rule-counter telemetry is operational firewall visibility; this UC does not assert an adversary technique)

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement contract

Assign a Linux firewall owner and a Splunk content owner. Inventory whether each host is managed through native nftables, the iptables-nft compatibility tools, or iptables-legacy. Configure exactly one collection path per host: collecting native nftables and iptables-nft views together can duplicate the same kernel policy, while mixing iptables-legacy and nftables can represent genuinely separate rulesets. Record the chosen value as `backend`.

This UC measures rule counters, not log records. Netfilter counters are cumulative unsigned packet and byte values. A single snapshot says how much a rule has seen since creation or reset; interval activity requires subtracting an earlier snapshot from a later snapshot. The packet counter counts rule matches, not unique connections. The byte counter is the byte count observed by that rule at its hook, not application payload, billed bytes, or throughput measured at an interface. Packets can traverse multiple counting rules, so cross-rule sums are not a unique-traffic total.

Give every managed rule one durable logical comment token, for example `splunk-rule-id=allow-ssh-prod`. The token is the human-governed identity and must be unique within a host/backend ruleset. For nftables, attach the token with the rule `comment` attribute and include exactly one inline `counter` statement. For iptables/ip6tables, use `-m comment --comment "splunk-rule-id=allow-ssh-prod"`; iptables already maintains counters for each rule. The reference collector deliberately ignores rules without an ID and nftables rules with zero, multiple, named, or shared counters. That narrow contract is auditable and avoids pretending a shared named counter belongs to one rule.

Identity has three layers. `rule_id` is the stable operator name. `rule_fingerprint` is a SHA-256 digest of the counter-free rule representation and changes when match/action semantics change. `native_rule_key` is `handle:<n>` for nftables or `position:<n>` for iptables. The SPL groups by all three plus host, boot ID, backend, family, table, and chain. This can sacrifice one interval when a harmless position changes, but it prevents a new native instance from being silently compared with an old one. No periodic snapshot can detect an identical iptables rule that is deleted and recreated entirely between polls when every observed identity component is unchanged; change monitoring is a separate control.

The collector needs permission to list the ruleset, commonly root or a tightly constrained capability/helper arrangement. Do not grant it permission to modify, flush, or reset rules. Review local privilege design with the platform security owner; a generic setuid wrapper is not supplied here. The Universal Forwarder runs the script locally and forwards stdout. On Splunk Cloud, the script still runs on the customer-managed forwarder, not on the managed search tier.

## Step 1 — Deploy and verify collection

Create a deployment-owned app such as `TA_linux_firewall_counters`; do not modify a vendor add-on. Place `scriptExample` at `bin/linux_firewall_rule_counter.py`, make it executable by the forwarder service identity, and invoke it with the selected backend:

```ini
[script://./bin/linux_firewall_rule_counter.py nftables]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
source = linux_firewall_rule_counter
sourcetype = linux:firewall_rule_counter
```

Use `iptables` instead of `nftables` only for the iptables interface. The script invokes commands without a shell, emits one compact JSON object per managed rule, uses one `sample_epoch` for the complete poll, and fails rather than inventing partial output when the command itself fails. Validate command paths in the forwarder's environment; if distribution packaging places them outside `PATH`, use reviewed absolute paths in the deployed copy.

Configure search-time JSON extraction in the search app:

```ini
[linux:firewall_rule_counter]
KV_MODE = json
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT
```

Do not also set `INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS=JSON`; Splunk documents that combining it with `KV_MODE=json` extracts fields twice. `_time` is ingestion time for operational searching, while `sample_epoch` is the collector's measurement time and is what the delta search orders and windows. Keep host clocks synchronized. Do not allow a rule comment to override Splunk's metadata `host` field.

Run the script as the forwarder service identity. There is no separate Netfilter vendor UI for this kernel state, so verify in the native command-line interface rather than inventing a console comparison. For nftables, compare each output event with the matching rule from `nft --json list ruleset`; confirm family, table, chain, handle, comment, packets, and bytes. For iptables, compare with `iptables-save --counters` and `ip6tables-save --counters`; the `--counters` option is what includes current packet and byte values. Confirm one event per managed rule and no event for an unmanaged rule. Search `index=os sourcetype=linux:firewall_rule_counter source=linux_firewall_rule_counter earliest=-10m | table _time sample_epoch host boot_id backend family table chain rule_id rule_fingerprint native_rule_key packets_total bytes_total` and expect approximately one sample per minute per rule.

The expected event count is `managed_rules × 1,440` per host per day at 60-second cadence. Measure actual event bytes and retention requirements in the target deployment; this review does not invent a GB/day estimate. If that cardinality is too expensive, reduce the managed rule set first. Increasing cadence changes timeliness and gap policy and must be accompanied by a search and test update.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the report

Save the primary SPL as `linux_firewall_rule_counter_delta_5m` and schedule it every five minutes on minute boundaries. Preserve `earliest=-20m@m latest=-4m@m`: the earlier data provides a predecessor snapshot, and the four-minute lag allows forwarding/indexing to settle. The candidate predicate selects samples ending from nine through five minutes before dispatch, which represent the five-minute measurement interval from ten through five minutes before dispatch when cadence is healthy.

`tonumber` rejects malformed counters by turning them null. The first `stats` collapses exact duplicate identity/sample rows with `max`; cumulative counters must never be summed at this stage. `sort 0` is mandatory because `streamstats` compares the immediately preceding event in result order. `current=f window=1` copies the previous sample only within the full rule-instance key. A reboot, changed semantics, moved native locator, or changed namespace starts a new series and therefore cannot inherit a prior counter.

An interval is comparable only when time advances and the gap is no more than 150 seconds. The upper bound tolerates ordinary one-minute jitter and one delayed/missed poll without presenting a long outage as current behavior. If either counter decreases, the interval is a reset. Because traffic before the reset and traffic after it cannot be separated from two snapshots, both packet and byte deltas are null for that interval. The search does not add the new post-reset total, take an absolute value, assume wrap, or clamp a negative delta to zero.

The final `stats` sums only valid adjacent deltas for one rule instance. `packets_delta` is packets and `bytes_delta` is bytes over the reported interval. Rates divide by measured elapsed seconds, not a presumed 300 seconds. A row with valid zero deltas is `no_hits`; a reset takes precedence as `counter_reset`. Keep `observed_intervals`, `measured_intervals`, `reset_intervals`, and elapsed time visible so consumers can distinguish silence from weak coverage.

This is a report, not a universal high-volume alert. Triggering on any hit would page on ordinary allowed traffic, while one global threshold would ignore rule purpose and host class. If operations later adds a threshold, place it after the final delta calculation, key it by exact rule identity, store threshold units explicitly as packets per five minutes, packets/s, bytes per five minutes, or bytes/s, and call it local policy rather than a Netfilter or Splunk default.

There is no CIM/tstats substitute. Event counts in a network data model count indexed events; they do not expose these cumulative kernel counters, reset boundaries, comments, fingerprints, or native rule instances.

## Step 3 — Validate counters, identity, resets, and windows

Run the positive control with six fixture events. Five adjacent increases of 10 packets and 1,000 bytes over 60 seconds must total 50 packets and 5,000 bytes over 300 seconds. The derived rates are approximately 0.167 packets/s and 16.667 bytes/s. Confirm all identity fields survive unchanged and `measurement_state=hits`. Use fixture `sample_epoch` values that fall in the search's candidate window relative to dispatch; do not rewrite `_time` and assume it controls ordering.

Run the zero-hit negative control. Six unchanged snapshots must return one `no_hits` row with five measured intervals and exact zero deltas. This proves the report distinguishes a valid idle rule from absent data. Then lower packets or bytes in one interval. The result must show one reset, only non-reset intervals may contribute deltas, and both rates must be null because the full aggregate window is not continuous. Manually verify one real pair as `new_packets-old_packets` and `new_bytes-old_bytes`.

Test identity boundaries independently: change `boot_id`; change only the nft handle or iptables position; change the fingerprint; reuse the logical ID in a different chain; and send the same logical ID from a different backend. Each must start or retain a separate series, never borrow the previous instance's counters. Create two different managed rules with the same logical ID on a test host and ensure the governance/data-quality check rejects the duplicate even though fingerprints keep search rows separate.

Test data quality: malformed numeric strings, a backward or duplicate `sample_epoch`, a 151-second gap, duplicate copies of one snapshot, one missing required identity field, command failure, and delayed indexing. Malformed or incomplete events must be excluded; nonpositive time and long gaps must not produce deltas; exact duplicates must not double counts; command failure must be visible in forwarder logs and as missing cadence, not zero-counter JSON.

For nftables, test a controlled `nft reset rule ...` or ruleset reload only in a lab/change window and verify reset behavior. For iptables, zeroing or restoring counters likewise creates a boundary. Never reset production counters merely to validate Splunk. Retain fixture events, expected rows, actual rows, search version, and reviewer sign-off. Documentation review and deterministic fixture design do not make the UC production-verified.

## Step 4 — Operationalize evidence and investigation

Build the primary table at rule grain. Keep packets and bytes in separate columns and label every rate axis. Add a zero-hit inventory sorted by time since last positive delta, a reset/change panel, and a collection-health panel showing last sample, interval counts, duplicate samples, fingerprint changes, and logical-ID collisions. For trends, chart one rule at a time or use small multiples; a stacked chart across rule traversal paths is easy to misread as unique traffic.

A zero-hit rule is a review candidate, not automatic proof that the rule is unnecessary: it may protect rare failover, incident-response, management, or seasonal paths. A high-hit rule can be expected. Investigation should review the exact rule expression and verdict, chain hook and ordering, adjacent rules, service ownership, approved scanners, retry behavior, and network telemetry. This feed does not carry source/destination fields, so pivot to packet logs, flow telemetry, conntrack, endpoint logs, or a controlled packet capture only when authorized.

Retain saved-report definitions, dispatch metadata, normalized measurements, identity registry, and reviewed dashboard exports according to operational policy. Record collector version and ruleset-management source because a fingerprint alone is not a human-readable policy explanation. If an auditor asks for proof of firewall effectiveness, state narrowly that these artifacts show observed rule-counter movement and monitoring continuity; they do not establish that every intended path was tested or that the policy satisfies a regulation.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and suppress safely

No events usually means the input is disabled, the command path is wrong, the forwarder identity cannot list rules, no selected rule carries a valid ID, nftables rules use named rather than inline counters, output routes to another index, or the search role lacks index access. Run the exact command and collector as the forwarder user, inspect `splunkd.log`, and verify effective configuration with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`.

Events with null fields indicate missing `KV_MODE=json`, a sourcetype mismatch, malformed JSON, or simultaneous index-time/search-time extraction. Missing deltas with healthy events usually mean there is no predecessor for that full identity, the native locator or fingerprint changed, timestamps did not advance, counters decreased, or the gap exceeded 150 seconds. Implausibly large deltas require checking host collisions, duplicate deployment ownership, mixed backend collection, stale sample clocks, and rule-ID reuse before assuming traffic volume.

Do not hide resets or zero-hit rules from the base report. Apply any downstream alert suppression only after deltas are complete, with exact identity and a bounded approved window. Filtering a raw snapshot before `streamstats` can cause the search to compare observations across the excluded interval and misattribute traffic, so pre-delta exception lookups are prohibited.
grandmaExplanation: We read the numbers beside each Linux firewall rule and work out how much they changed. That shows which rules are being used and which have stayed quiet, without recording every packet as a separate message.
